Background

Predict before you run.

TraceFirst is a first-year C++ tracer built on one rule: you never run code you have not first predicted — commit to an answer, then step through the program and watch where your prediction and the machine part. If you are new to programming entirely, start with Bolt's World, the first mode below: it teaches the logic first, and only then does the tracer ask you to predict real code.

Test-out check

Seven short questions, answered in order — no stepping, and each answer is final for this sitting. Score 6 or 7 and the opening stretch is marked as tested out: Start Here steps 1 to 3 tick, the primer counts as read, and Tracer Exercises 1 to 5 are marked Tested out. Retakes are unlimited, and a tested-out exercise can still be done normally later — your real attempt replaces the mark.

Meet the Code · Before the tracer

Meet the Code: what a program's lines are

Bolt gave you the logic. This is the same logic wearing real C++ clothing. Read the program once, line by line, with the note beside each line. There is nothing to predict yet, and nothing to run.

#include <iostream>

→This line brings in the tools for printing to the screen and reading input. Almost every program you meet here starts with it.

using namespace std;

→This lets the program write cout instead of std::cout. It appears once, near the top.

int main() {

→Every program starts running here, at main. The { opens the body of the program.

int score = 25;

→A statement: it makes a box named score and puts 25 in it. The ; ends the statement, the way a full stop ends a sentence.

score = score + 5;

→This reads the value in the box, adds 5, and puts the answer back in the same box.

cout << score;

→cout sends a value to the screen. The << points the way the value flows: out of the program, onto the screen.

return 0;

→main hands 0 back to the computer to say: finished, and nothing went wrong.

}

→This } closes the body of main. Every { must have its }.

Three rules to carry into the tracer

  • A semicolon ends a statement.
  • Braces { } group lines into one block.
  • The tracer will show you the boxes. Predict what is in them before you run.
Prediction Tracer

Reference card

Open it from anywhere, close it and your work is exactly where you left it.

Reference card — print me

The whole course on one page: operators, the integer-division rules, the vector and string methods this platform uses, and the loop patterns that recur everywhere. Formatted to print cleanly — use the Print this card button and only this card prints.

Operators

OperatorMeansWatch out
=Store the right side in the left boxIt is not a comparison. x = x + 1 reads the old x first.
==Compare: are they equal?The classic mix-up with = inside an if.
+= -= *= /=Update a box from its own valuetotal += v is total = total + v.
++ --Add / subtract 1As a statement, prefix and postfix behave the same.
&& || !And / or / not&& stops at the first false; || stops at the first true.
& * (pointers)&x is x's address; *p is the value p points atIn a declaration, int* p makes a pointer; in an expression, *p follows it.

Integer division rules

ExpressionResultWhy
17 / 53Both operands are int: the fraction is discarded (truncated, never rounded).
17 % 52The remainder that division threw away.
17 / 5.03.4One double operand makes the whole division double.
(double)17 / 53.4Converting one side before dividing has the same effect.

Vector & string methods used here

MethodDoes
v.push_back(x)Append x; the vector grows by one.
v.size() / s.length()How many elements / characters there are now.
v[i] / s[i]The element / character at index i, counting from 0.
s.substr(pos) / s.substr(pos, len)The text from pos to the end / for len characters.
counts[key]A map's slot for key — created at 0 on first use.
seen.insert(x) / seen.count(x)Add x to a set if absent / ask whether x is in the set (1 or 0).

Loop patterns

PatternShape
Counted loopfor (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { ... } — runs exactly n times.
Accumulatetotal = 0; before the loop, total += value; inside it.
Read to end of filewhile (fin >> value) { ... } — test the read, never eof() alone.
Walk a collectionfor (int v : values) { ... } — maps give pairs: p.first, p.second.
Modes

Meet Bolt — programming before the syntax gets heavy.

Bolt is a workshop robot who understands exactly four commands: move, turn left, pick up a battery cell, put one down. That is all he will ever know. Everything Bolt does — crossing the Workshop, harvesting a row of cells, feeling his way around crates — is built by combining those four commands with loops, decisions, and functions you define yourself.

The programs are written in real C++ shape: every command ends with a semicolon, blocks wear braces, and helpers are void functions. Nothing here is a toy language you will have to unlearn. When you move on to the Prediction Tracer, the syntax will already look familiar; only the ideas will be new.

Start here. This mode comes first on purpose: finish these twelve worlds and you already think in sequences, loops, decisions, and functions. Then predict and trace real code in the Prediction Tracer, where the same logic wears full C++ syntax.
Worlds — twelve workshops, in order
Bolt Challenges (optional) 6 extra worlds ▾

For students who finish the twelve worlds and want more. These challenges are entirely opt-in: they gate nothing and unlock nothing, and they use the same Workshop, the same editor, and the same Run, Step, and Reset controls below. Pick one to load it into the board.

Your program for Bolt

Write C++-shaped code: every command ends with a semicolon, and blocks wear braces. Lines starting with // are comments — notes to yourself that Bolt ignores.

Choose a world, write Bolt's program, then press Run or Step.

Bolt's command card

Commands — every one ends with ;

  • move(); — step one square the way Bolt is facing.
  • turnLeft(); — turn 90° to Bolt's left, staying on the same square.
  • pickCell(); — pick up one battery cell from the square Bolt is standing on.
  • putCell(); — put one cell from Bolt's bag down on his square.

Sensors — questions Bolt can ask

  • frontIsClear() — true when the square ahead is inside the Workshop and holds no crate.
  • cellsPresent() — true when a battery cell sits on Bolt's square.
  • Put ! in front to flip the answer: !frontIsClear() means “something is in the way.”

Patterns — decide, repeat, name

void turnRight() { turnLeft(); turnLeft(); turnLeft(); } while (frontIsClear()) { move(); } for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { pickCell(); }

Decide with if (cellsPresent()) { ... } else { ... }. Define a helper once with void name() { ... }, then call it anywhere with name();.

How Bolt's World fits: this mode teaches the logic of programming — sequence, repetition, decisions, decomposition — inside a world small enough to see whole. The other modes then attach real C++ to that logic: the Prediction Tracer for reading code before it runs, the Debugging Gym for finding faults, the Error Translator for compiler messages, and Challenges for graded practice. Worlds you complete are saved in this browser, on this device.

    Find the bugs. Classify them. Then prove the fix.
    
          
    Seven short programs, broken on purpose — the first three from a debugging and code-reading lab built for a first-year introductory C++ course serving CS and non-CS majors together, the rest extending the same hunt to loops, arrays, functions, and strings. Click a line to accuse it of being a bug. Every accusation that lands must then be classified, because the distinction this gym trains is the one beginners blur:
    
          
    
            
    Syntax errorThe code breaks a rule of the language. The compiler catches it and the program never runs.
    
            
    Logic errorThe code is legal, compiles clean, and still does the wrong thing. Only the output exposes it.
    
          
    
          
    
            By the end of the gym you can:
            
      
              
    • Read a program you did not write and locate its errors systematically, from a checklist, not by staring.
      • 
              
    • Distinguish syntax from logic errors, with an example of each.
      • 
              
    • Point the stream operators the right way: << out with cout, >> in with cin — and say why main() returns int.
      • 
              
    • Explain operator precedence, the semicolon that detaches an if, and why text needs string and getline.
      • 
            
    
          
    
        
    

        
    
          
    
            
    Rounds — seven broken programs, in order
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
        
    

        
    
          
          
    
          
    
          
    
          
    
            
    faulty.cpp — click a line to accuse itC++
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
          
    
            
    Bug found on line . Now classify it:
    
            
    
            
    
              
              
            
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
            Three false alarms — here is the checklist from the lab. Work the program top to bottom and ask, line by line:
            
      
              
    • Semicolons present — after every statement, including using namespace std and return 0?
      • 
              
    • Is main declared correctly — int main()?
      • 
              
    • Stream operators pointing the right way — << for output, >> for input?
      • 
              
    • Types chosen well — string, not char, for text of more than one character, and getline where the answer contains spaces?
      • 
              
    • Formulas right — and is a semicolon sitting directly after an if (condition), detaching its block?
      •

          Stage 3 of 4 · Fix · Stage 4 · Verify
          
    Fix the program yourself
    
          
    The faulty program again — but this time only the faulty lines are editable. Every other line is locked. There is no Run button here on purpose: when you press Check my fix, the machine runs your assembled program against this round's test (input: ). If it passes, the same program is immediately run against a second, unseen test — that is the Verify stage. One practical note: an editable line may hold more than one statement when a fix needs an extra step — for example, cin.ignore(); before a getline that follows a cin >> read.

    Read the error. It is telling you where to look.
    
          
    A compiler message is not a verdict. It is a note from the program that checks your code, written in shorthand. Pick the error you just hit, or search for a word in it, and TraceFirst will translate it into plain English: what it means, what in your code causes it, and how to fix it.
    
        
    

        
    
          Start here · From code to error to meaning
          
    One broken program, three real errors
    
          
    This is the kind of program a first week produces. It will not compile. The compiler stops and reports the three errors below — in this order. Tap any error to jump to its translation.
    
          
    
            
    firstProgram.cpp — will not compileC++
    
            
    1#include <iostream>
    2using namespace std
    3
    4int main() {
    5    int score = 85
    6    Cout << "Your score is " << scroe << endl;
    7    return 0;
    8}
    
          
    
          
    
            
            
            
          
    
          
    Fix them in order. Fix Error 1, compile again, and the list gets shorter. That loop — read, fix one, recompile — is the whole method.
    
        
    

        
    
          
    
            
            
    
              
              
            
    
          
    
          
    Showing all 32 errors — ordered by how early beginners usually meet them.
    
        
    

        
    
        
    No error matches that search. Try a single word from the message — declared, expected, token — or a cause like semicolon or quotes.
    

        
    The method: an error message names the line where the compiler gave up, which is not always the line where the mistake is; read the first error first, fix it, compile again.
    

        
    How to use this translator well: do not hunt through all 32. Copy two or three distinctive words from the message you actually got into the search box. The raw messages here use the wording of g++, the compiler in most introductory courses; other compilers phrase the same problems slightly differently, but the cause and the fix do not change.

          Student Labs — author & share Your own prediction exercises ▾
          
    
            
    Now set the trap yourself. Write a short program, run it to learn what it really prints, then name the wrong answer you expect a classmate to predict — and why it tempts them. Saving gives you a share code to hand over. Anyone pasting that code must predict first, in their own words, before the real output is revealed. There is no step-through for authored exercises: the reveal is the output itself, checked against your trap. Your authored exercises live in their own list below and never touch the tracer record, the accuracy counts, or the instructor digest.

    Bridge: from reading code to writing it.
    
          
    First put a program's lines in order, then write the missing lines yourself.
    
        
    
        
    
          
    
            
    Activities — Parsons and faded, in order
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
        
    
        
    
          
          
    
          
    
          
    
          
    
            
            
          
    
          
    Build or complete the program, then press Check. The machine runs what you assembled and compares what it prints.
    
        
    
        
    How Bridge fits: the tracer taught you to read programs other people wrote; Make asks you to write whole programs from a blank editor. Bridge is the rung between them — first ordering lines, then supplying them — and it judges by behaviour: any arrangement or line that makes the program print the right thing passes.
    
      
    

      
    
        
    
          
    Make: write and run your own C++
    
          
    Prediction taught you to read the machine; this is where you write for it. Pick a prompt, write the whole program yourself in the editor, and run it right here. Then put it through the prompt's test bench: the machine runs your program once per test and compares what it prints with what the prompt asks for.

    Output
    
          
    
            
    Test bench
    
            
    
            
    Run tests feeds each test's input to a fresh run of your program and compares the printed output, ignoring differences in spacing. Some prompts also have hidden tests: you see only how many of them passed, never their inputs or expected outputs. A prompt counts as complete when every visible and every hidden test passes.
    
          
    
          
    
            
    Work the way you learn best
    
            
    
              
              
              
            
    
            
    Test-driven mode reveals this prompt's tests one at a time: the next test unlocks only when the current one passes. Completion still requires every visible and hidden test. Real mentoring and a community solutions gallery belong to the later platform phase; the local slice here is test-driven mode, curated alternative solutions, and the style checklist.

    Lecture mode — run a tracer exercise in front of the class
    
            
    A single projected screen: pick any of the 37 exercises, tally the class's predictions as counts, see the live split, then step through with the split pinned beside the trace. It is a facilitator view on this device only — tallies are kept in memory for the session and are never added to any student's record or to the digest below.
    
            
    
          
    
                    
    
            
    Instructor exercise studio
    
            
    Author a tracer exercise in the same C++ subset the Make interpreter runs. The true output is never typed in: it is taken from an actual run of your code, and saving stays blocked until the current code has run cleanly. On save you also get a share code (TFI1:) another instructor can load below. Saved exercises appear in the Prediction Tracer's exercise list under Instructor-authored, labelled I1, I2, … — the 37 built-in exercises keep their numbers. Instructor-authored attempts never touch the built-in exercises' records, accuracy counts, Start Here route, test-out state, or the digest counts.

    Instructor digest — where the class parted
    
          
    Paste one or more exported journals below, or load journal files, then build the digest. It aggregates attempts per exercise, counts wrong predictions, and surfaces the most common wrong prediction and parting line for each exercise. Rows where anyone missed are highlighted.
    
          
    
            
            
            
    
              
              
            
    
            
    
              
              
            
    
            
    
          
    
          
    
        
    
      
    

      
    How TraceFirst works: each exercise follows PRIMM — Predict, Run, Investigate, Modify, Make — the teaching sequence set out by Sentance, Waite and Kallia (2019) in computing-education research. The prediction is not a quiz before the lesson; it is the lesson, because the step-through that follows is read against a model you have already committed to.
